en: Semetey came there in flight.
Kanykei arrived a wanderer;
Semetey arrived an orphan.
Temir Khan gave his command;
When Temir Khan commanded,
His people did not oppose him.
Then the khojas in white turbans,
The mullahs who taught their lessons:
'For this daughter who has come wandering,
Temir Khan has acted wisely,' they said.
'While mighty Manas was alive,
He offended his daughter;
Now he has drawn her to his side
And made her close to him,' they said.
The multitude of Bukhara, ruled by a sovereign,
Once their khan had given his command,
Did not make him say it twice.
'The noble khan's offspring,
Straying and fleeing to Bukhara,
Has come here wandering,' they said.
The people approved his words
And now agreed to his wishes.
There were nine hundred households
Together in Bukhara;
These he now set apart for her.
They now agreed to his wishes;
He now sent word to his people.
Over nine hundred households,
Though a woman, the unfortunate one
They now raised as khan.
They draped her in silk,
Mounted her on a smooth-gaited pacer;
Sixty women, eighty girls—
So many stood about her.
That dear mother of yours, Kanykei,
Had fled to Bukhara.
When first she fled there,
She had lost her fierce warrior,
At the age of thirty-two.
Bereft of Khan Manas,
She saw a night that would not turn back.
To Temir Khan's city
She wandered and made her living.
To the walled city of Bukhara,
Bereaved, she fled and sustained her life.
She saw a moonless night;
Bereft of her precious one,
She lived through days of devastation.
With nine hundred households under her hand,
The people's mouths were silenced.
Kanykei remained in mourning;
Semetey entered Bukhara and was raised there.
Such was the command God had sent;
She now saw it was so.
Without calling the orphan her child,
She gave him wholly to her brother,
To Ismayil.
He never wore a coat draped over his back.
Manas, who had gone to the other world—
He had no idea this was his father.
The dear land called Talas—
He had no idea this was his homeland.
Kanykei, who went in mourning—
He had no idea the poor woman was his mother.
At that time, Semetey,
Temir Khan's dear camel calf,
Ismayil's son,
That orphan left by Manas,
Had his mind on other things.
Many years passed between;
If you looked, the days had passed.
He prospered by plundering riches;
Semetey grew up in Bukhara.
The orphan grew to maturity;
He joined the ranks of men.
No one could torment him;
The bold lad who took after his father—
None remained who could turn him with a catching pole.
He proved a burning ember;
He proved a thundering bullet.
In the great city of Bukhara,
Damn him, no such troublemaker had ever appeared!
When he reached twelve,
He imprisoned any mendicant he saw
And beat the wandering dervishes.
Unable to endure his mischief,
The whole city of Bukhara grew weary.
He proved a lion protected by Shay;
All twelve parts of his body grew in perfect balance.
One day there was turmoil in Bukhara.
The khojas in white turbans,
The mullahs who taught their lessons,
Looked about in fear and grieved.
The reason for their grief was this:
Eighty khojas and a hundred mullahs
He shut inside their mosque.
The notorious troublemaker Semetey
Beat every one alike.
The khojas wept in anguish;
The mullahs' heads were split.
The people of Bukhara took counsel
And ran this way and that.
'I shall die!' they cried, despairing of life.
The people grieved;
Many heads were split.
With their belts around their necks,
They ran in flustered haste;
Their knees bent to the ground.
They ran this way and that,
Following along his path.
He had reached twelve;
They all denounced Semetey alike.
When the people gathered, upon their necks
Lay a heavy, painful burden.
The wretched people ran about in distress;
They complained to his father, Temir Khan.
Following along his path,
All the foolish, wretched people
Let loose together,
Denouncing him to his grandfather Temir Khan.
Before Temir Khan,
The wretched people gathered round;
These were the words they spoke:
'My lord, an ember has risen from the hearth!
Here in the city of Bukhara,
A great bully named Semetey has appeared.
The people cry out in grief.
The khojas in striped coats,
The most accomplished mullahs—
Many of their heads were split.
When his anger rises, Bukhara
This orphan of yours holds prisoner.
Any khoja who falls into his hands
He beats until he screams.
My lord, dislike us if you will:
Cut down the willow by the stream!
He is bursting into flame;
Restrain that orphan of yours.
If you do not restrain this orphan,
Bukhara, that great city with its gates—
We shall not dwell within it.
Twice a day, morning and evening,
If your orphan keeps amusing himself with us,
We shall not recover from his cruelty.
He has reached twelve this year;
At fifteen he will leave us no peace,
He will leave none of us unharmed.
He will plunder our riches.
If your orphan keeps going like this,
He will stir up great disorder.
If this orphan goes on like this,
He will not let us turn our ploughs.
May I have no share if I am lying:
He will not let us remain in Bukhara.
If his terrible frenzy takes hold,
The boy will cause a slaughter.
With thimble mouths and camel-calf eyes,
The playfully swaying girls—
He will take them as spoils like this
And drive them away to the Kyrgyz.
He will not let us turn our ploughs.
May I have no share if I am lying:
He will not let us remain in Bukhara.
He will not let us ready our yoke-pins.
If this orphan lives,
He will not let us plough in summer.
He will not let us open the face of the earth,
He will not let us scatter seed widely.
When summer comes,
If this orphan lives,
He will not let us ride a maned mare.
When autumn comes,
If this orphan keeps thundering,
He will not let us eat a fat-tailed lamb.
He sends your khojas scurrying into hiding,
Beats your mullahs like sheep,
And raids your mares.
This orphan will bring forth—
You are in Kapkay.
Come near him and see:
He punches till your brains are scattered.
Consider it, my lord:
Concealed malice lies in his eyes.
If you speak sharply and firmly,
He is ready to strike you down.
He descends from one who chased white deer
And made them cattle.
The whole wide world—
He descends from one who threw it into turmoil.
Driving and chasing gray deer,
His forebear made them cattle.
Every land he set his sights upon—
His forebear threw it into turmoil.
He set grassy places afire,
Kindled the meadowlands,
Poured blood into clear waters,
Greased the rivers.
Whoever provoked his enmity,
He seized and slew.
He never abandoned his greed;
Asking for food, he was never sated.
Sent out into the darkness,
He prowled like a leopard.
This damned boy is Kyrgyz stock.
My lord, either let him stay in Bukhara,
Or let us stay in Bukhara.
His mother Kanykei
Trotted like a hunting hound;
Having suffered great hardship,
She came wandering from Talas.
Because she had no means,
She cut the twig,
Performed the customary rite,
And gave him to Ismayil.
The orphan you have raised
Has reached twelve years old.
He dug great trenches,
Made the poor souls boil with misery,
Stripped many people of their coats.
He meant to bring upon Bukhara
Unheard-of wonders.
He meant to draw the line,
He meant to bring upon Bukhara
Relentless excitement.
Smashing the city of Bukhara,
He meant to make the calamity greater.
Cut down the willow of this land;
My lord, restrain your orphan.
If you do not restrain your orphan,
We shall scatter our treasure and property,
And flee wherever we turn our faces.
If your orphan carries on like this,
What shall we do staying here?
We shall leave in every direction.'
When the people came crying out,
Temir Khan in Bukhara,
Once he had heard the people's complaint,
Turned his attention to it.
He almost massacred
The royal city of Bukhara.
Those who spoke harshly,
He locked in his dungeon.
Those who answered him insolently—
He seized them and beat them.
He shouted a proclamation,
Summoned the assembled people.
As the proclamation rang out,
The multitude of Bukhara—
Commanders of ten came bobbing,
Commanders of fifty came jutting forth;
The swordsmen held themselves timidly,
The axe-bearers stood hushed.
They took their places in a row.
Temir Khan, enraged,
Now spoke these words:
'Your elders with swan-white beards—
